nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Light reaching the canopy drives the forest; little of it reaches the shaded floor, where herbs and seedlings compete for gaps.

nodes.name: Equatorial rainfall
nodes.desc: Year-round rain feeds the rivers and keeps the forest wet; it is the water supply for every plant here.

nodes.name: Seasonal flooding
nodes.desc: Rivers such as the Salonga, Lokoro and Lula spill into swamp and flooded forest, creating wetland habitat for sedges, palms and fish.

nodes.name: Forest soil and leaf litter
nodes.desc: Fallen leaves, fruit and dead animals are broken down here, and the nutrients are taken up again by roots.

nodes.name: Fungi and bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down dead plants and animals in the warm, wet forest floor and return nutrients to the soil.

nodes.name: Velvet tamarind trees
nodes.desc: Forest trees whose fruit is eaten by bonobos. Seeds that pass through a bonobo can germinate better, and some Dialium seem to rely on that.

nodes.name: Fig trees
nodes.desc: Fig trees produce fruit that feeds birds, monkeys, apes and elephants, which then carry the seeds away.

nodes.name: Marantaceae herbs
nodes.desc: Broad-leaved herbs of the forest floor and clearings, grazed by forest elephants. Marantochloa congensis is recorded near the park.

nodes.name: Raffia palms
nodes.desc: Palms of swamps and wet ground. Their fruit is a main food of the palm-nut vulture.

nodes.name: Swamp sedges and aquatic grasses
nodes.desc: Sedges and reeds along flooded edges and clearings. They are staple food for the sitatunga.

nodes.name: African forest elephant
nodes.desc: Eats bark, leaves and many kinds of fruit, and spreads large seeds far from the parent tree. Hunting is the main threat in Salonga.

nodes.name: Bonobo
nodes.desc: Eats mostly fruit, plus leaves, invertebrates and some small animals. It is the second-largest fruit eater in the Congo forest and a major seed disperser.

nodes.name: Black crested mangabey
nodes.desc: A forest monkey recorded in the park area. Monkeys of this kind are prey of leopards and crowned eagles.

nodes.name: Black-casqued hornbill
nodes.desc: About 90% fruit, with figs and oil palm fruit as staples, plus some insects. It spreads the seeds of many trees.

nodes.name: Congo peafowl
nodes.desc: Endemic to the Congo Basin and found in both old and regrowing forest in Salonga. Eats fruit, insects, spiders, snails and worms.

nodes.name: Forest insects and snails
nodes.desc: Beetles, termites, ants and other small animals of the leaf litter. They feed on plants and decaying matter and are eaten by many birds, fish and reptiles.

nodes.name: Sitatunga
nodes.desc: A swamp antelope that feeds on sedges, fresh grasses and herbs at wetland edges. It hides in deep water, partly submerged, when threatened.

nodes.name: Forest river fish
nodes.desc: Salonga holds dozens of fish species. They feed on insects and other small animals and are the main food of dwarf crocodiles in the Congo basin.

nodes.name: Congo dwarf crocodile
nodes.desc: A small nocturnal crocodile of forest streams and swamps. In the Congo it eats mostly fish, with more crustaceans in the dry season.

nodes.name: Nile monitor
nodes.desc: A water-loving lizard recorded near the park. Eats fish, crabs, frogs, eggs, small animals and invertebrates, as well as carrion.

nodes.name: Palm-nut vulture
nodes.desc: An unusual vulture that lives mainly on oil and raffia palm fruit, but also takes fish, crabs, frogs and carrion.

nodes.name: Leopard
nodes.desc: Takes monkeys and duikers. Leopards are among the few predators of bonobos and sitatunga.

nodes.name: Crowned eagle
nodes.desc: Rainforest eagle that hunts mostly monkeys, including mangabeys, and also takes hornbills and monitor lizards.
